item.title: Explore Pods
item.description: In this tutorial you build a single NGINX Pod in Kanvas, deploy it to a live cluster, expose it with a NodePort Service, and inspect the running Pod in Operator: its details, a shell inside its container, and its log stream. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules, and every workload controller you meet later (Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs) exists to create and replace Pods. Working with a bare Pod first shows you exactly what those controllers automate.

item.title: Open an Interactive Terminal
item.description:
The interactive terminal opens a shell inside a running container without leaving the Operator canvas. Use it for last-mile diagnosis that logs and status cannot answer: testing connectivity from inside a pod, reading a mounted file, or checking an injected environment variable. It is a browser-based equivalent of kubectl exec, scoped to the resource you selected.

Before you start 🔗

  • Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode. See How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud.
  • A connected cluster with Meshery Operator deployed. Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and a message broker in the cluster. MeshSync executes the shell, and Meshery Server relays input and output through the broker. If any of the three is unavailable, the terminal does not connect (see Failure modes).
  • A running container whose image contains /bin/sh. Distroless images have no shell and cannot be used.

Open a session 🔗

The action is named Initiate Terminal Session and is offered on Pod and Container resources only. Right-click the resource on the canvas, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel. The session starts immediately and the terminal panel opens at the bottom left of the canvas. There is no separate connect step.

item.title: Explore Deployments
item.description: In this tutorial you build an NGINX Deployment with two replicas, deploy it, scale it to three, and roll it to a new image version, inspecting the result in Operator after each change. A Deployment is the controller most stateless applications run under: you declare how many Pods you want and what they look like, and Kubernetes keeps that many running and replaces them gradually when the template changes. Seeing the ReplicaSets and Pods appear and change shows you what the controller does on your behalf.

item.title: Stream Container Logs
item.description:
Log streaming live-tails the output of a pod’s containers inside the Operator canvas. Each stream starts with the most recent lines and then follows new output as it is written, so you can watch a rollout, a crash loop, or a request path next to the topology that produced it.

Before you start 🔗

  • Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode.
  • A connected cluster with Meshery Operator deployed. MeshSync reads the logs and Meshery Server relays them through the broker, the same path the terminal uses. See Operator.
  • Containers that exist. Logs come from the Kubernetes log API, so a container that has not started has nothing to stream.

Start a stream 🔗

The action is named Initiate Log Session and is offered on Pod and Container resources only. Right-click the resource, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel. The stream opens in the same bottom-left panel as terminal sessions, as a tab.

item.title: Explore Services
item.description: In this tutorial you put three Services in front of running workloads: a ClusterIP Service in front of a Deployment, a NodePort Service in front of one Pod, and a LoadBalancer Service in front of another. Pods come and go and change IP addresses every time they are replaced. A Service gives a changing set of Pods one stable address and finds them by label, and its type decides who can reach that address. Building all three side by side makes the difference between the types concrete.

item.title: Run a Performance Test
item.description:
Operator mode shows a live picture of your clusters. A performance test adds the missing signal: how a service responds under load. You select a Service or Ingress on the canvas, Kanvas seeds a test from it, and Meshery runs the load and keeps the result as a reusable performance profile.

Before you start 🔗

  • Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode.
  • A target Meshery Server can reach. Meshery Server generates the load, not your browser and not the cluster. The address you test must be routable from wherever Meshery Server runs. A ClusterIP address is reachable from inside the cluster only.
  • Performance permissions. The form needs View performance profiles to appear, and the Run Test button needs Run test. See Permissions by Role.

Start a test 🔗

The action is named Initiate Performance Test and is offered on Service and Ingress resources only, the kinds that expose an endpoint. It is not offered on pods, deployments, or any other kind. Right-click the resource, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel.

item.title: Deploy AWS EC2 Instances
item.description: In this tutorial you create a VPC network and EC2 instances in your AWS account without leaving Kanvas. You deploy three designs from the catalog, in order, to your own Kubernetes cluster: a controller that talks to AWS, a VPC network, and the EC2 instances that run inside it. Each AWS resource is a Kubernetes custom resource in the design, and a controller in the cluster turns that resource into real infrastructure.

item.title: Deploy Azure Resources
item.description:
In this tutorial you install Azure Service Operator (ASO) in your own Kubernetes cluster, then design an Azure resource group and a storage account inside it, deploy both from Kanvas, and find them in the Azure portal. You manage real Azure infrastructure with the same design, validate, and deploy loop you use for Kubernetes workloads, and the cluster keeps that infrastructure matched to the design.

The trade-off is indirection. Kanvas never calls Azure. It applies Kubernetes objects to your cluster, and ASO turns those objects into Azure resources in the background. A successful deploy means the cluster accepted the objects; the Azure resources follow a little later, and Azure-side failures surface on the objects in the cluster, not in the deploy summary.

item.title: Operator
item.description:
Operator mode is Kanvas’s view of what is running. Designer mode works on what you intend to run. Operator draws the Kubernetes resources found in your connected clusters on the same canvas, shows each one’s recorded state, and gives you actions against the live workloads: open a shell, follow logs, run a load test, or jump back to the design that produced a resource.

Where Operator data comes from 🔗

Kanvas does not talk to your clusters directly. Four pieces sit between a cluster and the canvas:

item.title: Operate Infrastructure
item.description:
These guides cover tasks you run against live clusters from Operator mode. Each task starts from a resource on the Operator canvas and runs through Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and the broker that Meshery Operator deploys in the cluster. To see how those pieces fit together, read Operator.

To do this Resource kinds Guide
Open a shell in a running container Pod, Container Open an Interactive Terminal
Follow a pod’s or container’s logs Pod, Container Stream Container Logs
Generate load against an endpoint Service, Ingress Run a Performance Test

Operator mode needs a Meshery deployment that can reach your clusters. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer it.

item.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
item.description:
Kanvas binds every shortcut to both modifier keys. On Windows and Linux use Ctrl. On macOS use Cmd. The tables write the modifier as Ctrl/Cmd.

Kanvas ignores shortcuts while you type in a text field, so typing a label, a comment or a search never triggers one. Open the same list inside the app with Ctrl/Cmd + /.

Modes and navigation 🔗

Shortcut Action Designer Operator
V or Esc Switch to the Select tool. Esc also closes open menus and dialogs. Yes Yes
H Switch to the Pan tool. Yes Yes
Space (hold) Pan while the key is down, then return to the Select tool. Yes Yes
Ctrl/Cmd + P Turn the Pencil tool on or off. Yes No
Ctrl/Cmd + E Turn the Pen tool on or off. Yes No
Ctrl/Cmd + + Zoom in. Yes Yes
Ctrl/Cmd + - Zoom out. Yes Yes
\ (backslash) Open the Layers panel. Yes Yes
Ctrl/Cmd + / Open the shortcut reference in the help drawer. Yes Yes
Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + / Open the Help Center. Yes Yes

The tools are described in Tool Modes.

item.title: Operator Views
item.description:
A view is to Operator mode what a design is to Designer mode: a named, saved definition you reopen later. A view stores which resources to show, not the resources themselves. Opening a view re-applies its filters to the current inventory of your connected clusters.

What a view stores 🔗

Field Content
Name Defaults to Untitled View. Up to 255 characters. Not required to be unique.
Filters Kinds, models, namespaces, labels, and the name search text. See Filters.
Visibility public or private.
Notes Free text (Markdown) in the view’s metadata, edited in View Info.
Owner, created, updated Set by Layer5 Cloud.

A view does not store layout, zoom, pan, or the selected resource. It does not store cluster selection either: the clusters selected in the Meshery context selector at the time you open the view always win. A copied link includes your current pan and zoom as URL parameters, but they are not saved in the view.

item.title: Resource Details
item.description:
Selecting a resource on the Operator canvas opens the Details panel. It shows the resource as Meshery last recorded it from the cluster, and it carries the actions that apply to that kind. Fields with no value are omitted, so each kind shows only what applies.
